title: Warmth gave no clear repeated change in traffic slopes for recorded frog composition in four US samples in 2006-2015
abstract: We tested whether warmer survey air changed the passing-car association with recorded frog composition. We used 80,092 stop visits on 613 Northeast and Midwest US NAAMP routes in 2006-2010 and 2011-2015. The outcome was mean detection of green frogs and bullfrogs minus mean detection of American toads and the gray treefrog complex. Models controlled survey runs, sites by survey window, local temperature, and state and month traffic slopes. Changes in the zero-to-five-car contrast per 5 C ranged from -0.33 to +1.41 percentage points per species. All four 98.75 percent route-cluster intervals included zero. Observer, traffic-limit, listening-break, state-year and stop-order checks gave no repeated clear change. Three designs did not identify a planned average traffic contrast, although all four identified the warmth interaction. Those unsupported averages are not reported. Selected nights, few years, capped traffic counts, mixed gray treefrog labels and unmeasured calling and hearing limit inference. This is a weather and observation test, not a causal climate, true occupancy or chemical air-pollution result. Code, exact source hashes, a derived CC0-source panel, aggregate results and independent solver checks support reproduction.

display.caption: Left: change per 5 C in the fitted zero-to-five-car low-minus-comparison detection contrast, in percentage points per species. Blue intervals use route clusters with 98.75 percent nominal coverage. Orange intervals use the largest of route, year and two-way errors with five-year t quantiles. Right: observed traffic support. Separate regions and periods share one survey program; periods can share routes.

citations.reason: We adapt its baseline MIT fixed-effect and covariance code and audit pattern. Its outcome was summed richness with subjective impairment. We test acoustic class balance with car counts and a different region-period split. Raw observations overlap.
Earlier calling-season evidence motivates a weather-dependent observation test. We adopt its Northeast and Midwest state lists. Source observations overlap.
Prior road-salt models used traffic as a detection control. We test traffic by warmth for a fixed acoustic-class contrast, not salt effects. The source archive overlaps.
Foreman, Grant and Weir (2017), USGS NAAMP release. Runs, stops, counts and metadata supply all inputs. The release page marks the data CC0.
Eastern Ontario individual-call study motivates the fixed green frog and bullfrog versus toad and gray treefrog comparison. We do not reuse its measurements or copyrighted materials.
Traffic-noise masking in gray treefrogs shows that the comparison class is not noise-immune.
